section_summary: This section opens with the continuation of a numbered digest of Domei reports on economic administration, public works, trade, agriculture and industrial self-sufficiency across Japanese-occupied Southeast Asia. It then contains Federal Communications Commission cover letters and raw English or romanized-Japanese radio intercepts carrying Domei war news and propaganda about China, the Philippines, Burma, India, French Indochina and the Pacific war. Recurring subjects include the Indian National Army, Allied air raids, colonial concessions in Shanghai, infrastructure and resource development, and Japanese relations with Southeast Asian governments.

subfiles.title: Domei Press digest: Philippines through French Indochina, items 102–149
subfiles.from: Domei News Agency reports; compiler not stated
subfiles.about: A numbered digest reports economic, administrative and industrial developments in Japanese-occupied Southeast Asia during July 1943.
subfiles.summary: The surviving portion begins in the Philippines and continues through the Netherlands East Indies, Malaya, Burma, Thailand and French Indochina. Reports emphasize public works, agricultural and industrial self-sufficiency, resource exploitation, banking, transport and Japanese administrative reforms. The French Indochina portion also describes commodity agreements with Japan, price and trade controls, official appointments and fishing-port construction.

subfiles.title: FCC cover letter transmitting intercepted Domei Press, 14 July 1943
subfiles.from: G. E. Sterling, Federal Communications Commission Radio Intelligence Division
subfiles.to: Adolf A. Berle Jr., Assistant Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Sterling forwards additional copies of Domei Press broadcasts intercepted from Japanese stations.
subfiles.summary: The confidential letter accompanies a group of radio-intercept transcripts. It identifies FCC file 12718 and State Department decimal-file number 894.76/138.

subfiles.title: Intercepted Domei Press broadcast, 9 July 1943
subfiles.to: Federal Communications Commission Radio Intelligence Division
subfiles.about: The broadcast combines Japanese war claims and propaganda with reports from the Philippines, China and French Indochina.
subfiles.summary: Items announce Alejandro Roces's death, renewed Pearl River navigation, Japanese claims concerning fighting near Roviana and Munda, and a Canton account of American bombing casualties. A long report describes Chinese river-control, canal, reclamation and highway projects around the Yellow River, Jiangsu and Nanjing. The final items allege civilian casualties near Haiphong and announce additional Philippine post offices.

subfiles.title: Intercepted Domei Press broadcast, 8 July 1943
subfiles.to: Federal Communications Commission Radio Intelligence Division
subfiles.about: This broadcast reports Japanese military claims and promotes the Indian National Army and Japanese-sponsored administration in Burma.
subfiles.summary: The opening items concern Philippine telephone exchanges and Japanese claims about fighting near Salamaua, Nassau Bay and Bobdubi. Several items celebrate Subhas Chandra Bose, the Indian Independence League and the newly organized Indian National Army in Singapore. Other reports cover Japanese–Thai cultural missions and alleged economic and administrative progress in Burma.

subfiles.title: Domei intercept fragment on Shanghai and the invasion of Sicily
subfiles.to: Federal Communications Commission Radio Intelligence Division
subfiles.about: A fragment reports the impending return of Shanghai concessions and the Axis response to the Allied landing in Sicily.
subfiles.summary: Domei intercept fragment: the scheduled return of Shanghai's International Settlement and French Concession to Chinese control, and a Rome report of the Allied attack on Sicily and claimed Allied aircraft losses.

subfiles.title: FCC cover letter transmitting intercepted Domei Press, 16 July 1943
subfiles.from: G. E. Sterling, Federal Communications Commission Radio Intelligence Division
subfiles.to: Adolf A. Berle Jr., Assistant Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Sterling forwards another group of Domei Press broadcasts intercepted from Japanese stations.
subfiles.summary: FCC confidential cover letter (file 12718, 894.76/139) for Domei Press intercepts of July 16, 1943.

subfiles.title: Romanized-Japanese Domei broadcast on the Canton air raid
subfiles.to: Federal Communications Commission Radio Intelligence Division
subfiles.about: The romanized-Japanese broadcast condemns American bombing of Canton and identifies purported American airmen lost there.
subfiles.summary: The report presents a Canton ceremony and aircraft donation as expressions of Japanese and Chinese anger over American bombing. It attacks American casualty claims and lists Howard C. Allas, M. L. Lewis, Paul G. Webb, James Young and other airmen allegedly shot down near Hong Kong or Canton.

subfiles.title: Romanized-Japanese Domei broadcast on political unrest in India
subfiles.to: Federal Communications Commission Radio Intelligence Division
subfiles.about: The broadcast discusses railway sabotage, casualties and legislative opposition to British rule in India.
subfiles.summary: Romanized Domei broadcast: a New Delhi report alleges Indian authorities hid the seriousness of a railway bombing that derailed a train, and a legislative demand to repeal an antiwar resolution and ease treatment of imprisoned leaders.

subfiles.title: Intercepted Domei Press broadcast, 10 July 1943
subfiles.to: Federal Communications Commission Radio Intelligence Division
subfiles.about: The broadcast ranges from Philippine reconstruction and Franco-Japanese negotiations to Pacific-war propaganda and Indian National Army recruitment.
subfiles.summary: Initial items cover rebuilt bridges in Luzon, Japanese deposits, the Shanghai French Concession and commodity negotiations with French Indochina. A long commentary argues that the American Pacific offensive was driven by the need to regain rubber, tin and other resources and would overextend United States forces. Later reports concern airmail in the East Indies, employment for Filipino prisoners of war, the Indian National Army, Japanese naval victory claims and a posthumous citation for Shigeru Nakasaki.

subfiles.title: Intercepted Domei Press broadcast, 9 July 1943
subfiles.to: Federal Communications Commission Radio Intelligence Division
subfiles.about: The broadcast promotes Subhas Chandra Bose and reports Japanese claims about Chinese troop surrenders and American air operations.
subfiles.summary: Domei, July 9, 1943: Indian Independence League volunteers leave Canton for Singapore, Bose visits memorials and adopts "Jai Hind," and a Nanjing review claims many Chongqing troops surrendered and describes American raids on Canton, Lingling and Liangshan.

subfiles.title: Intercepted Domei Press broadcast, 8 July 1943
subfiles.to: Federal Communications Commission Radio Intelligence Division
subfiles.about: The broadcast reports Japanese officials' travel and celebrates Tojo's review of the Indian National Army in Singapore.
subfiles.summary: Items announce Iwane Matsui's arrival from Bangkok and Sotaro Ishiwata's consultations in Shanghai. Newspaper coverage of the Indian National Army is described in detail, followed by an account of Hideki Tojo reviewing the force with Subhas Chandra Bose.

subfiles.title: Intercepted Domei Press broadcast on Manila arrests and New Guinea development
subfiles.to: Federal Communications Commission Radio Intelligence Division
subfiles.about: The broadcast reports arrests in a Manila murder case and outlines Japanese plans to exploit New Guinea's labor and resources.
subfiles.summary: The Manila item says three alleged terrorists led by Beverino Go were arrested for murdering Chinese Residents Society vice-chairman Cheng Han-chi. Magohei Tanaka's New Guinea report describes mobilizing 200,000 inhabitants for mining, agriculture, fishing, shipbuilding, resin tapping, oil extraction and soap manufacture in support of the Japanese war effort.

subfiles.title: Intercepted Domei Press fragment, 10 July 1943
subfiles.to: Federal Communications Commission Radio Intelligence Division
subfiles.about: The fragment covers employment for released Filipino prisoners, new schools in Cebu and negotiations over Shanghai concessions.
subfiles.summary: Domei, July 10, 1943 fragment: over 3,000 released Filipino prisoners found work via welfare units; Cebu middle schools would replace English with Japanese; an incomplete item on Ambassador Tani's talks with Henri Cosme over Shanghai's Settlement.

subfiles.title: FCC cover letter transmitting intercepted Domei Press, 20 July 1943
subfiles.from: G. E. Sterling, Federal Communications Commission Radio Intelligence Division
subfiles.to: Adolf A. Berle Jr., Assistant Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Sterling forwards additional Domei Press intercepts to the State Department.
subfiles.summary: FCC confidential cover letter (file 12718, 894.76/140) for Domei Press intercepts of July 20, 1943.

subfiles.title: Romanized-Japanese broadcast on wartime shipping reorganization
subfiles.to: Federal Communications Commission Radio Intelligence Division
subfiles.about: The romanized-Japanese text describes emergency reorganization of Japan's wartime maritime transport system and assigns operating responsibilities among shipping companies.
subfiles.summary: Romanized broadcast argues tighter state coordination and corporate responsibility would raise shipping capacity, and lists regular-line, tramp, tanker and special-service concerns designated for operations.

subfiles.title: Intercepted Domei Press broadcast, 11 July 1943
subfiles.to: Federal Communications Commission Radio Intelligence Division
subfiles.about: The broadcast reports maritime training in Java, disrupted communications near Turkey and a coal strike in Pennsylvania.
subfiles.summary: A Jakarta item says thirty youths were selected for seamen's training and announces another institute at Semarang. A Lisbon report claims the Turkish–Syrian border and Bulgarian–Turkish telephone links had been closed. The Buenos Aires item describes a widening Pennsylvania miners' strike, government use of the Connally–Smith Act and around-the-clock picketing.

subfiles.title: Intercepted Domei Press broadcast, 12 July 1943
subfiles.to: Federal Communications Commission Radio Intelligence Division
subfiles.about: The broadcast reports an American air raid in Tonkin and a meeting between Ba Maw and Hideki Tojo.
subfiles.summary: Domei, July 12, 1943: Indochina authorities report bombing and strafing near Lao Cai and the Tonkin coast with casualties, and Ba Maw thanks Tojo for Burmese independence and discusses wartime cooperation.

subfiles.title: Intercepted Domei Press broadcast, 14 July 1943
subfiles.to: Federal Communications Commission Radio Intelligence Division
subfiles.about: The surviving page covers a Thai information delegation's Japanese tour and begins a Manila commentary attacking American propaganda.
subfiles.summary: Domei, July 14, 1943: Thai officials Pairot Jaiyanama and Prichanusat Panyarachun arrive in Japan to inspect facilities; Thai ambassador Direck Jayanama praises Tojo's Bangkok visit; the page ends in a Taliba commentary ridiculing American propaganda in the Philippines.
